label_policy: `proposed` labels are PROVISIONAL model suggestions. They are never ground truth and the harness never scores against them. Authoritative labels live only in human_labels.json.
domain_limitation: All evidence is reused stored evidence from the SQLite/PostgreSQL development runs. This claim set is a single-domain verification test set: it is NOT a cross-domain evaluation and says nothing about other domains.

label_rules.title: Evidence boundary
label_rules.text: Judge ONLY the cited text exactly as shown on the review sheet (that is what the verifier receives, cut at 1,500 characters, which cuts none of these). Ignore other parts of the page, other passages and what you know. A frozen example has no neighbouring-passage context; the production pipeline adds neighbours.

label_rules.title: Decompose the claim
label_rules.text: List every assertion: entities, numbers, dates, scope words (always, only, all, at most), hedges and attribution (who said it).

label_rules.title: contradicted
label_rules.text: The shown text explicitly states something incompatible with an assertion of the claim (a different number or date, the opposite status, a negation, a different named entity). An explicit evidential contradiction takes precedence over partial support: if any assertion is explicitly contradicted, label contradicted even when another assertion is established. Something merely implied or merely not mentioned is never a contradiction.

label_rules.title: Precedence when parts disagree
label_rules.text: First apply R3: an explicitly contradicted assertion makes the claim contradicted. Only when no assertion is explicitly contradicted: if at least one assertion is established AND at least one other is missing, stronger, broader or more certain than the text, label partially_supported. partially_supported therefore means support that is incomplete or overstated WITHOUT explicit contradiction. Supported never wins when any part fails.

label_rules.title: Weaker core versus stronger claim
label_rules.text: When the text establishes the claim's central fact but in a weaker form (a suggestion stated as a rule, a list entry stated as the largest, a hedge dropped), label partially_supported.

label_rules.title: unsupported
label_rules.text: The text does not establish the claim's central fact: off-topic, a genuine quote that says nothing about it, a typical use case restated as a limit, a plan or forecast restated as something that happened, a different assertion on the same topic.

label_rules.title: Attribution
label_rules.text: A claim that attributes a statement or recommendation to its source ('Tinybird says ...') is judged on whether the source says it. A claim that states a source's opinion, ranking or forecast as plain fact is not fully supported.

changed_rules.R3: The shown text states something incompatible with the claim (a different number or date, the opposite status, a negation, a different named entity) AND no assertion of the claim is established. A single-assertion claim whose assertion is explicitly opposed is contradicted. Something merely implied or merely not mentioned is never a contradiction.
changed_rules.R4: If at least one assertion is established AND at least one other is missing, stronger, broader, more certain or explicitly contradicted, label partially_supported. A contradicted part does NOT make the whole claim contradicted when another part is supported (this follows the verifier's rule for bundled claims). Supported never wins when any part fails.

label_rubric_history.change: An explicit evidential contradiction takes precedence over partial support. partially_supported applies when support is incomplete or overstated without explicit contradiction. R3 and R4 were rewritten; R1, R2, R5, R6 and R7 are unchanged.
label_rubric_history.reason: v1 R4 said a contradicted part next to a supported part is partially_supported, while the reviewer's decision for CE16 (one figure matches, one is explicitly contradicted) was contradicted. The two could not both be applied, so the rule was reconciled before any label was imported.
label_rubric_history.verifier_note: When v2 was adopted the product verifier's bundled-claim sentence ('any that the evidence does not establish makes the claim partially_supported') conflicted with it. It was aligned afterwards as verifier rubric attribution-v2 (backend/claims.py RUBRIC_HISTORY): an explicit contradiction of any asserted part takes precedence. Verdicts made earlier keep their stamp attribution-v1 and are not rewritten. A scripted test checks the instruction text and output schema, not model judgment.
label_rubric_history.labels_affected: No human label existed when v2 was adopted (nothing had been imported), so no confirmed label changed under v2.
label_rubric_history.held_out_note: Held-out CE19 has the same shape (supported part plus an explicitly contradicted part). Its provisional label and its v1 annotation are deliberately left as written; it is reviewed with the other held-out examples, not before.

CE13.why: Public domain is supported; 'accepts contributions from anyone' is explicitly opposed by the text (the project is not open-contribution). Under v2 R3 the explicit contradiction takes precedence.

CE16.why: The 156,000 figure matches; the test-code figure (920 million vs 92 million) is explicitly contradicted. Matches the reviewer's stated decision (contradicted); the provisional label still shows the v1 result.

label_review_log.reason: Re-reviewed on the exact text the verifier receives: the central fact (a key customer) is established, only the ranking is not. This example is in the held-out split; the change is to a provisional label, made before any run or human review.

label_review_log.reason: Same re-review: the suggestion is established, 'always' is not.

label_review_log.to: ambiguity notes plus the deciding rule
label_review_log.reason: Labels unchanged. Each ambiguity is now decided by a stated rule, using the exact verifier-visible text, and the remaining reason for hesitation is kept.

independence_note: Passages with cited_by_development_claims=true were cited by claims in the Phase 3/4 development runs. The held-out split is independent in its CLAIMS only, not in its evidence sources.

wikipedia_sqlite:P16.text:
SQLite uses automated regression testing prior to each release. Over 2 million tests are run as part of a release's verification. The SQLite library has 156,000 lines of source code, while all the test suites combined add up to 92 million lines of test code. SQLite's tests simulate a number of exceptional scenarios, such as power loss and I/O errors, in addition to testing the library's functionality. Starting with the August 10, 2009 release of SQLite 3.6.17, SQLite releases have 100% branch test coverage, one of the components of code coverage. SQLite has four different test harnesses: the original public-domain TCL tests, the proprietary C-language TH3 test suite, the SQL Logic Tests, which check SQLite against other SQL databases, and the dbsqlfuzz proprietary fuzzing engine.[46]

wikipedia_sqlite:P9.text: SQLite stores the entire database, consisting of definitions, tables, indices, and data, as a single cross-platform file, allowing several processes or threads to access the same database concurrently. It implements this simple design by locking the database file during writing.[20] Write access may fail with an error code, or it can be retried until a configurable timeout expires. SQLite read operations can be multitasked, though due to the serverless design, writes can only be performed sequentially. This concurrent access restriction does not apply to temporary tables, and it is relaxed in version 3.7 as write-ahead logging (WAL) enables concurrent reads and writes.[21] Since SQLite has to rely on file-system locks, it is not the preferred choice for write-intensive deployments.[22]

postgresql_docs:P5.text: Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution. In effect, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run. However, SELECT does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed. Also note that two successive SELECT commands can see different data, even though they are within a single transaction, if other transactions commit changes after the first SELECT starts and before the second SELECT starts.

postgresql_docs:P21.text: To guarantee true serializability PostgreSQL uses predicate locking, which means that it keeps locks which allow it to determine when a write would have had an impact on the result of a previous read from a concurrent transaction, had it run first. In PostgreSQL these locks do not cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock. They are used to identify and flag dependencies among concurrent Serializable transactions which in certain combinations can lead to serialization anomalies. In contrast, a Read Committed or Repeatable Read transaction which wants to ensure data consistency may need to take out a lock on an entire table, which could block other users attempting to use that table, or it may use SELECT FOR UPDATE or SELECT FOR SHARE which not only can block other transactions but cause disk access.

postgresql_docs:P26.text:
When the system is forced to combine multiple page-level predicate locks into a single relation-level predicate lock because the predicate lock table is short of memory, an increase in the rate of serialization failures may occur. You can avoid this by increasing max_pred_locks_per_transaction, max_pred_locks_per_relation, and/or max_pred_locks_per_page.

A sequential scan will always necessitate a relation-level predicate lock. This can result in an increased rate of serialization failures. It may be helpful to encourage the use of index scans by reducing random_page_cost and/or increasing cpu_tuple_cost. Be sure to weigh any decrease in transaction rollbacks and restarts against any overall change in query execution time.

wikipedia_sqlite:P8.text: Due to the serverless design, SQLite applications require less configuration than client–server databases. SQLite is called zero-configuration[19] because configuration tasks such as service management, startup scripts, and password- or GRANT-based access control are unnecessary. Access control is handled through the file-system permissions of the database file.[20] Databases in client–server systems use file-system permissions that give access to the database files only to the daemon process, which handles its locks internally, allowing concurrent writes from several processes.

In PostgreSQL, you can request any of the four standard transaction isolation levels, but internally only three distinct isolation levels are implemented, i.e., PostgreSQL's Read Uncommitted mode behaves like Read Committed. This is because it is the only sensible way to map the standard isolation levels to PostgreSQL's multiversion concurrency control architecture.

The table also shows that PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads. This is acceptable under the SQL standard because the standard specifies which anomalies must not occur at certain isolation levels; higher guarantees are acceptable. The behavior of the available isolation levels is detailed in the following subsections.

To set the transaction isolation level of a transaction, use the command SET TRANSACTION.

wikipedia_sqlite:P6.text:
In August 2000, version 1.0 of SQLite was released, with storage based on gdbm (GNU Database Manager). In September 2001, SQLite 2.0 replaced gdbm with a custom B-tree implementation,[a] adding transaction capability. In June 2004, SQLite 3.0 added internationalization, manifest typing, and other major improvements, partially funded by America Online. In 2011, Hipp announced his plans to add a NoSQL interface to SQLite, as well as announcing UnQL, a functional superset of SQL designed for document-oriented databases.[15]

SQLite is one of four formats recommended for long-term storage of datasets approved for use by the United States Library of Congress.[16][17][18]

Design

[edit]

wikipedia_sqlite:P5.text:
Many programming languages have bindings to the SQLite library. It generally follows PostgreSQL syntax, but does not enforce type checking by default.[8][9] This means that one can, for example, insert a string into a column defined as an integer. Although it is a lightweight embedded database, SQLite implements most of the SQL standard and the relational model, including transactions and ACID guarantees.[10] However, it omits many features implemented by other databases, such as materialized views and complete support for triggers and ALTER TABLE statements.[11]

History

[edit]

D. Richard Hipp designed SQLite in the spring of 2000 while working for General Dynamics on contract with the United States Navy.[12] Hipp was designing software used for a damage-control system aboard guided-missile destroyers; the damage-control system originally used HP-UX with an Informix database back-end. SQLite began as a Tcl extension.[13]

postgresql_docs:P17.text:
The Repeatable Read isolation level is implemented using a technique known in academic database literature and in some other database products as Snapshot Isolation. Differences in behavior and performance may be observed when compared with systems that use a traditional locking technique that reduces concurrency. Some other systems may even offer Repeatable Read and Snapshot Isolation as distinct isolation levels with different behavior. The permitted phenomena that distinguish the two techniques were not formalized by database researchers until after the SQL standard was developed, and are outside the scope of this manual. For a full treatment, please see [berenson95].

Note

Prior to PostgreSQL version 9.1, a request for the Serializable transaction isolation level provided exactly the same behavior described here. To retain the legacy Serializable behavior, Repeatable Read should now be requested.

postgresql_docs:P18.text:
The Serializable isolation level provides the strictest transaction isolation. This level emulates serial transaction execution for all committed transactions; as if transactions had been executed one after another, serially, rather than concurrently. However, like the Repeatable Read level, applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures. In fact, this isolation level works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions. This monitoring does not introduce any blocking beyond that present in repeatable read, but there is some overhead to the monitoring, and detection of the conditions which could cause a serialization anomaly will trigger a serialization failure.

public_export.hash_policy: Content that is published can be re-hashed here. Withheld content keeps the hash recorded on the original: text_sha256 / quote_sha256 for passages and quotes, claim_sha256 for a withheld claim text, claim_sha256_full_evidence for the claim-plus-evidence hash that labels and the split lock use. Those retained hashes cannot be verified from this export.
public_export.note: Text of the withheld passages is not published. Hashes below let a holder of the full evidence verify it. Claim texts (except the two in claims_withheld), proposed labels, split assignment and the split lock are unchanged; for an example with withheld evidence the claim hash recorded on the full evidence is used, so human labels and the held-out lock keep their meaning. Anything that needs the evidence text refuses such an example unless an available-evidence subset is selected explicitly.
